title: Instant Pot Korean-Style Dakbokkeumtang with Chicken & Potatoes
dek: Bone-in chicken, potatoes and carrots pressure-braise in a glossy gochujang sauce, with sweet potato noodles and table-side heat for a flexible family supper.
image_alt: Korean chicken and potato stew in a red gochujang broth with glass noodles, carrots, scallions and sesame seeds
ingredients: 2 1/2 lb bone-in, skinless chicken thighs and drumsticks
1 medium yellow onion, cut into 1-inch wedges
1 1/2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
2 medium carrots, cut diagonally into 1/2-inch pieces
3 oz Korean sweet potato glass noodles (dangmyeon)
Gochugaru or chile crisp, optional for serving

instructions.name: Season the chicken and soak the noodles
instructions.text: Pat the chicken dry and season it with 1 teaspoon salt. Put the glass noodles in a heatproof bowl, cover with very hot water and soak for 20 minutes while you build the stew; drain well.

instructions.name: Sauté the aromatics
instructions.text: Select Sauté Normal on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Heat the oil, add onion and cook for 3 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds.

instructions.name: Deglaze to a clean base
instructions.text: Pour in 1 cup chicken broth and scrape the heating plate until no browned bits remain. Cancel Sauté, then add the remaining 1/2 cup broth. Layer potatoes, carrots and chicken into the thin liquid.

instructions.name: Float the seasoning above the liquid
instructions.text: Whisk gochujang, soy sauce, mirin, brown sugar, sesame oil and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Spoon this mixture over the chicken; do not stir it down onto the heating plate.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 8 minutes; allow about 12 minutes for the cooker to reach pressure. Keep the contents below the two-thirds line and do not reduce the 1 1/2 cups thin broth.

instructions.name: Release in two stages
instructions.text: Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes. Vent the remainder in short controlled pulses, keeping hands and face away from steam. If liquid sputters, close the valve, wait 2 minutes and resume more slowly. Open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Verify the chicken
instructions.text: Move several chicken pieces to a clean plate and check their thickest portions without touching bone; every piece must reach 165°F. If any is cooler, return it to the simmering sauce on Sauté until it reaches 165°F.

instructions.name: Finish the noodles and serve mild-first
instructions.text: Set Sauté Normal. Stir in the drained noodles and scallions and simmer 5 to 7 minutes, turning gently, until the noodles are tender and the sauce is glossy. Return the chicken, scatter with sesame seeds and offer gochugaru or chile crisp at the table.

why_it_works: A full 1 1/2 cups of thin broth goes onto a completely deglazed base before the thick gochujang seasoning is floated on top, reducing burn-warning risk.
Large potato pieces and bone-in chicken tolerate the eight-minute pressure cycle, while pre-soaked glass noodles finish afterward instead of absorbing the cooker liquid needed to seal.
The shared stew uses moderate gochujang for color and savory sweetness; optional gochugaru or chile crisp lets each diner choose the heat.
swaps: Use all bone-in chicken thighs of similar size; keep the same pressure time and verify every piece reaches 165°F.
For a noodle-free supper, omit the dangmyeon and simmer the sauce for 3 to 5 minutes after pressure until lightly reduced.
Replace mirin with 2 tablespoons apple juice plus 1 teaspoon rice vinegar for an alcohol-free balance.
storage: Cool in shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat chicken and sauce to 165°F, adding broth because the noodles continue to absorb liquid. Freeze the chicken, vegetables and sauce without noodles for up to 2 months; thaw overnight and add fresh soaked noodles while reheating.
notes: Total time includes about 12 minutes to reach pressure, the 8-minute cook, a 10-minute natural release and 5 to 7 minutes for the noodles.
Follow your exact model manual for minimum liquid, locking and venting. Do not exceed the two-thirds line or double this recipe in a 6-quart cooker.
Gochujang brands vary in heat and salt. Two tablespoons keeps the family pot moderate; pass extra heat at the table.
Never force the lid. Open only when the float valve has dropped completely.

faqs.a: Yes. Use 2 pounds boneless thighs, pressure-cook for 6 minutes and keep the 10-minute natural release. Verify every piece reaches 165°F before serving.

faqs.q: Why are the glass noodles added after pressure?
faqs.a: Dangmyeon absorb a great deal of liquid. Finishing soaked noodles after release preserves the thin liquid required for pressure and keeps them from turning overly soft.
It is traditionally a chile-forward stew, but gochujang intensity varies. This family version starts moderate and puts gochugaru or chile crisp on the table for diners who want more heat.

title: Instant Pot Romanian-Style Sarmale with Beef, Pork & Rice
dek: Tender cabbage rolls hold a savory beef, pork and rice filling, then pressure-braise over sauerkraut and arrive with creamy polenta and sour cream.
image_alt: Romanian cabbage rolls filled with meat and rice beside yellow polenta and sour cream
ingredients: 1/2 cup uncooked long-grain white rice, rinsed and well drained
1/4 cup chopped fresh dill, plus more for serving

instructions.name: Soften the cabbage leaves
instructions.text: Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Core the cabbage and lower it carefully into the water. As the outer leaves soften, remove 12 large leaves with tongs, 6 to 8 minutes total. Cool, then shave the thick center rib from each leaf without cutting through it. Chop 2 cups of the remaining cabbage.

instructions.name: Build the filling
instructions.text: Select Sauté Normal on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Heat oil and cook onion for 4 minutes. Add garlic and stir 30 seconds; transfer to a large bowl and cool 5 minutes. Mix in rice, beef, pork, egg, 1 teaspoon salt, thyme, paprika, pepper and dill just until combined.

instructions.name: Roll twelve sarmale
instructions.text: Place about 1/3 cup filling near the stem end of each cabbage leaf. Fold the sides inward and roll snugly, leaving a little room for the rice to expand. Keep the raw-meat filling and finished rolls away from ready-to-eat foods and wash hands and tools well.

instructions.name: Build a thin pressure base
instructions.text: Add 1 cup broth to the cooker and scrape the heating plate completely smooth. Cancel Sauté. Spread 1 cup sauerkraut and the chopped cabbage over the bottom. Arrange the rolls seam-side down in two snug layers.

instructions.name: Layer the sauce without stirring
instructions.text: Whisk tomato paste into the remaining 1/2 cup broth. Pour it over the rolls, add bay leaves and cover with the remaining sauerkraut. Do not stir the thick tomato mixture down to the heating plate.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook below the half-full line
instructions.text: Check that rolls, liquid and sauerkraut remain below the cooker's half-full line because the rice expands. Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 18 minutes; allow about 12 minutes to reach pressure.

instructions.name: Release naturally, then vent
instructions.text: Let pressure release naturally for 15 minutes. Vent the remainder in short controlled pulses, keeping hands and face away from steam. If the valve sputters, close it, wait 2 minutes and resume slowly. Open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Cook the polenta
instructions.text: While pressure releases, bring 4 cups water and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt to a boil in a saucepan. Whisk in polenta, reduce heat and cook according to package directions, usually 5 to 8 minutes. Stir in butter and keep warm.

instructions.name: Verify the centers and serve
instructions.text: Lift rolls carefully with a slotted spoon. Insert an instant-read thermometer through the side into the center of several rolls; each must reach 160°F. Simmer any cooler rolls in the hot broth on Sauté until they reach 160°F. Serve two rolls per person with polenta, sour cream, broth and extra dill.

why_it_works: Blanched leaves roll without tearing, while a modest one-third-cup filling leaves space for the rice to expand inside each parcel.
A full 1 1/2 cups of broth and moisture-rich cabbage sit against a clean heating plate; concentrated tomato paste stays diluted and above the rolls to reduce burn risk.
A 15-minute natural release lets the rice finish hydrating and prevents the fragile rolls from being battered by an immediate rush of steam.
swaps: Use all ground beef or all ground pork while keeping the total meat at 1 1/2 pounds and verifying the roll centers reach 160°F.
Replace sauerkraut with 2 additional cups thinly sliced fresh cabbage and add 1 tablespoon apple cider vinegar to the broth.
Serve with mashed potatoes instead of polenta; cook them separately so the pressure-cooker fill and liquid ratios remain unchanged.
storage: Cool rolls, broth and polenta in shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate rolls in their broth up to 4 days and polenta separately up to 3 days. Reheat the rolls to 165°F. Freeze rolls and broth, without polenta or sour cream, for up to 3 months and thaw overnight before reheating.
notes: Total time includes cabbage blanching and rolling, about 12 minutes to reach pressure, the 18-minute cook, a 15-minute natural release and polenta cooked during release.
Rice makes this an expanding-food recipe: stay below the half-full line and do not double it in a 6-quart cooker.
Follow your exact model manual for minimum liquid, locking and venting. Never force the lid or cover the steam valve with a towel.
Ground-meat fillings are safe at 160°F; check several rolls in their centers because exterior cabbage temperature does not prove the filling is done.

faqs.q: Can I assemble sarmale a day ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Arrange the uncooked rolls in a covered container and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Add them to the cooker cold, keep the same pressure time and verify 160°F centers.

faqs.q: Why is the cooker limited to half full?
faqs.a: The raw rice expands and the cabbage can foam. The conservative half-full limit gives that expansion room and follows the usual model guidance for grains and other foaming foods.

faqs.q: Can I use brown rice in the filling?
faqs.a: Not as a direct swap. Brown rice needs substantially more time and liquid than the meat and cabbage. Use cooked brown rice, cooled promptly, and reduce the amount to 3/4 cup cooked.

title: Dutch Boerenkool Stamppot with Smoked Sausage & Mustard
dek: Fluffy potatoes and kale mash into a buttery Dutch comfort-food supper topped with hot smoked sausage and a bright spoonful of mustard.
image_alt: Dutch kale and potato stamppot topped with sliced smoked sausage and yellow mustard
ingredients: 2 1/2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
12 oz chopped kale, tough stems removed
1 1/2 lb fully cooked smoked sausage or kielbasa
2 tbsp whole-grain or Dijon mustard, plus more for serving

instructions.name: Layer the potatoes and kale
instructions.text: Put potatoes in a large Dutch oven, cover with cold water by 1 inch and add 1 teaspoon salt. Pile kale on top, cover and bring to a boil. Reduce to a steady simmer and cook 18 to 22 minutes, until potatoes crush easily with a fork and kale is tender.

instructions.name: Heat the sausage
instructions.text: During the final 10 minutes, nestle the fully cooked sausage on top of the kale, cover and steam until its center reaches 165°F. Move it to a clean board and tent loosely with foil.

instructions.name: Warm the dairy
instructions.text: Heat milk and butter in a small saucepan or microwave-safe cup until steaming and the butter melts; do not boil.

instructions.name: Drain very well
instructions.text: Drain the potatoes and kale in a colander. Return them to the hot Dutch oven over low heat for 1 minute, shaking gently, so excess water evaporates.

instructions.name: Mash and season
instructions.text: Add the hot milk-butter mixture, remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, pepper, nutmeg and 2 tablespoons mustard. Mash until the potatoes are fluffy but some kale texture remains. Add another splash of milk only if needed.

instructions.name: Slice and serve
instructions.text: Slice the sausage into thick coins and arrange over the stamppot. Scatter with scallions if using and pass more mustard at the table.

why_it_works: Kale steams above the potato water, tenderizing without requiring a second pot or washing away its flavor.
Drying the drained vegetables over low heat prevents watery mash, while warm milk and butter absorb smoothly.
Heating the intact sausage with the vegetables keeps it juicy and turns a simple mash into a complete family meal.
swaps: Use a fully cooked chicken or turkey smoked sausage and reheat it to 165°F in the same way.
Replace kale with 12 ounces finely shredded green cabbage; simmer it with the potatoes until fully tender.
For dairy-free stamppot, use unsweetened plain oat milk and plant-based butter.
storage: Cool within 2 hours and refrigerate the stamppot and sausage in separate shallow containers up to 4 days. Reheat both to 165°F; loosen the mash with milk or broth. Freeze the mash up to 2 months, though the potatoes may be slightly grainier after thawing.
notes: Choose a package labeled fully cooked. Raw sausage needs separate cooking according to its package and a safe-temperature check appropriate to the meat.
Yukon Gold potatoes give the mash body without becoming as gluey as overworked russets; mash by hand rather than in a food processor.
Mustard is traditional at the table and also lifts the rich sausage and butter in the mash.

faqs.a: Boerenkool means kale and stamppot describes a Dutch dish of potatoes mashed with vegetables. This version pairs that mash with smoked sausage and mustard.
Yes. Thaw 12 ounces, squeeze it very dry and add it during the final 10 minutes of the potato simmer so the finished mash does not become watery.

faqs.q: Why did my stamppot turn gluey?
faqs.a: Overworking potatoes releases excess starch. Drain and dry them well, add warm dairy, and stop hand-mashing as soon as the texture is cohesive.

title: Puerto Rican Mofongo with Garlic Shrimp
dek: Crisp-fried green plantains mash with garlic into individual mofongo bowls, ready to catch tender shrimp and a savory lime-brightened pan broth.
image_alt: Puerto Rican fried plantain mofongo surrounding garlic shrimp, onions and peppers in a golden savory broth
ingredients: 1 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails optional
3 cups neutral oil, or enough for 2 inches in a heavy pot
1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken or seafood broth, divided
Lime wedges and hot sauce, optional for serving

instructions.name: Season and chill the shrimp
instructions.text: Pat shrimp dry and toss with 1/4 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Refrigerate while preparing the plantains.

instructions.name: Peel and cut the green plantains
instructions.text: Trim both ends, score each peel lengthwise without cutting deeply into the flesh and pry away the peel. Cut plantains into 1-inch rounds.

instructions.name: Fry the plantains
instructions.text: Heat neutral oil in a heavy pot to 325°F, keeping the pot no more than half full. Fry plantains in batches for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until golden and tender but not crisp. Maintain 300°F to 325°F and transfer with a slotted spoon to a rack or paper towels.

instructions.name: Start the garlic shrimp broth
instructions.text: Thinly slice 4 garlic cloves and finely grate the remaining 4. Heat olive oil in a wide skillet over medium. Cook sliced garlic, onion and bell pepper for 4 minutes. Add 1 cup broth, oregano, 1/4 teaspoon salt and remaining 1/4 teaspoon pepper; simmer 5 minutes.

instructions.name: Mash four mofongo portions
instructions.text: Working while the plantains are hot, pound one-quarter of them with one-quarter of the grated garlic, 2 tablespoons warm broth and a pinch of the remaining salt in a pilón or sturdy bowl. Stop at a cohesive, rustic mash. Pack into a lightly oiled small bowl, invert onto a warm serving bowl and repeat for four portions.

instructions.name: Cook the shrimp safely
instructions.text: Bring the skillet broth to a steady simmer. Add shrimp in one layer and cook 2 to 4 minutes, turning once, until opaque and 145°F at the thickest part. Remove the skillet from heat immediately.

instructions.name: Finish and serve
instructions.text: Stir lime juice and cilantro into the shrimp broth. Spoon shrimp, onions, peppers and plenty of broth around each mofongo. Serve at once with lime wedges and hot sauce at the table.

why_it_works: Frying thick plantain rounds at a moderate 325°F cooks their centers before their surfaces become too hard to mash.
Warm broth hydrates the fried plantains a spoonful at a time, producing a cohesive but still rustic mound that can absorb the shrimp sauce.
Shrimp cook only at the end and come off the heat at 145°F, so the garlic broth develops first without making them rubbery.
swaps: Use vegetable broth for a pescatarian base; choose a low-sodium broth so the plantain mash and shrimp can be seasoned separately.
For a pork-inclusive traditional variation, pound 1/2 cup crushed chicharrón into the plantains and reduce the added salt to taste.
If you do not have a pilón, use a sturdy mixing bowl and potato masher, working in four small batches while the plantains are hot.
storage: Mofongo is best immediately. Refrigerate cooled plantain mash and shrimp broth separately within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat the shrimp and broth gently to 165°F and warm the mash covered with a splash of broth; do not refry. Freezing is not recommended for the shrimp.
notes: Use firm green plantains, not yellow sweet plantains; their starch is what gives mofongo its savory structure.
For frying safety, keep the pot no more than half full, dry plantains well, monitor the oil with a thermometer and never leave hot oil unattended.
The photograph shows a generous golden broth with visible shrimp, onion and green pepper; spoon the sauce around, not only over, each plantain mound.

faqs.a: You can, but the result is drier and less traditional. Toss the rounds with 2 tablespoons oil, air-fry at 375°F until tender and golden, then add warm broth gradually while mashing.

faqs.q: Why will my plantains not hold together?
faqs.a: They may have cooled or need moisture. Mash them while hot and add warm broth one tablespoon at a time until the mixture packs firmly without becoming wet.

faqs.q: How do I avoid overcooking the shrimp?
faqs.a: Build and season the broth first. Add shrimp only to the simmering finished broth, turn once and remove the skillet from heat as soon as the thickest pieces reach 145°F.

title: Australian Lamingtons with Chocolate & Coconut
dek: Light vanilla sponge squares get a thin chocolate coating and a snowy coconut finish, with a chill-and-dip method that keeps the crumb neat.
image_alt: Square Australian lamington sponge cakes coated in chocolate icing and shredded coconut beside a cup of tea
ingredients: 6 tbsp unsalted butter, melted and cooled
2/3 cup whole milk, plus up to 2 tbsp if needed
3 cups (240 g) unsweetened fine shredded coconut

instructions.name: Prepare the pan and oven
instructions.text: Heat oven to 350°F. Grease an 8-inch square metal pan, line the bottom and two sides with parchment and lightly grease the paper.

instructions.name: Mix the dry ingredients
instructions.text: Whisk flour, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl until evenly combined.

instructions.name: Whip the eggs and sugar
instructions.text: Beat eggs and granulated sugar with an electric mixer on high for 4 to 5 minutes, until pale, thick and ribboning. Beat in vanilla.

instructions.name: Fold a light sponge batter
instructions.text: Sift half the flour mixture over the eggs and fold gently. Fold in half the milk, then repeat with remaining flour and milk. Fold a scoop of batter into the cooled melted butter, then fold that mixture back into the bowl just until no streaks remain.

instructions.name: Bake and cool completely
instructions.text: Spread batter evenly in the pan. Bake 23 to 27 minutes, until the top springs back, a tester is clean and the center is about 200°F to 205°F. Cool in the pan 10 minutes, turn onto a rack, remove parchment and cool fully.

instructions.name: Chill and cut
instructions.text: Wrap the cooled cake and refrigerate for at least 1 hour. Trim the edges if desired, then use a serrated knife to cut sixteen 2-inch squares. Put a rack over a rimmed sheet pan and place coconut in a shallow bowl.

instructions.name: Make a fluid chocolate icing
instructions.text: Sift confectioners' sugar and cocoa into a wide bowl. Whisk in melted butter, 2/3 cup milk, vanilla and salt until smooth. Add up to 2 tablespoons more milk as needed; icing should flow off a fork in a thin ribbon.

instructions.name: Dip, coat and set
instructions.text: Using two forks, lower one chilled cake square into the icing, turn to coat and let excess drip away. Roll gently in coconut and place on the rack. Repeat, reheating the icing over warm water if it thickens. Let lamingtons set for 30 minutes before serving.

why_it_works: Whipped whole eggs provide lift, while the butter is first lightened with a small amount of batter so it folds in without collapsing the foam.
A one-hour chill firms the sponge, producing clean squares that shed fewer crumbs into the chocolate icing.
A deliberately fluid cocoa icing soaks only the surface before coconut catches it, preserving a pale, tender center.
swaps: Use unsweetened desiccated coconut for the classic fine coating or shredded coconut for a more textured finish.
Replace whole milk with unsweetened oat milk and use a baking-style plant butter for a dairy-free version; the flavor will be slightly different.
For jam-filled lamingtons, split each chilled square horizontally, spread with 1 teaspoon raspberry jam and reassemble before dipping.
storage: Keep set lamingtons in a single layer in an airtight container at cool room temperature for 2 days or refrigerate up to 5 days. Bring to room temperature before serving. Freeze the uncoated cake up to 2 months; thaw, chill and coat. Coated cakes can be frozen but the coconut softens.
notes: Total time includes about 75 minutes for cooling and chilling plus 30 minutes for the finished coating to set.
Do not taste raw batter because raw flour and eggs can contain harmful bacteria; bake the cake fully before sampling.
If the icing collects crumbs, strain it through a fine sieve between batches and keep the remaining cake squares cold.

faqs.q: Why are my lamingtons crumbling in the icing?
faqs.a: The cake may be warm or too fresh. Cool it completely, chill for at least an hour, cut with a serrated knife and dip quickly with forks rather than squeezing the squares.

faqs.q: Can I bake the sponge the day before?
faqs.a: Yes. Cool it fully, wrap airtight and refrigerate overnight. A day-old chilled sponge is especially easy to cut and coat.

faqs.q: Why is my chocolate coating too thick?
faqs.a: Confectioners' sugar absorbs moisture as it sits. Whisk in warm milk one teaspoon at a time or set the bowl over warm water until the icing again falls in a thin ribbon.
